title: How do canopy cover and composition feed back onto longleaf pine growth and survival, understory community composition, and fuel bed flammability?
section: Chapter 1: Do light and fire synergistically control stand density?
text:
Chapter 1: Do light and fire synergistically control stand density?





This chapter of my dissertation is on-going, involving a multi-year observational study set up in the Sandhills of North Carolina. This work aims to determine:

How does light availability relate to growth of bolting longleaf pines?
How does size relate to survival?

title: How do canopy cover and composition feed back onto longleaf pine growth and survival, understory community composition, and fuel bed flammability?
section: Chapter 2: How does pyrophytic oak density relate to fuel load and fuel bed composition, and therefore flammability?
text:
Chapter 2: How does pyrophytic oak density relate to fuel load and fuel bed composition, and therefore flammability?





I have just started working on this chapter of my dissertation. This work aims to determine:

How does pyrophytic oak density relate to the fuel load and the relative abundance of fuel types in the understory?
How does the fuel load and relative abundance of fuel types shape fuel bed flammability and fire behavior?

title: Erin Emott
text:
I’m a 4th year PhD candidate at North Carolina State University, working with Bill Hoffmann. My research focuses on population-, community-, and ecosystem-level responses to variation in stand density and canopy composition in longleaf pine ecosystems.
I’m also the Treasurer of the Plant Biology Graduate Student Association, a Grad Peer Mentor through the College of Agriculture and Life Sciences, and a studio potter and ceramics teacher at the NC State Craft Center.
